## Why This Matters

L01 made a promise in its FAQ: *most data-science questions fit on a laptop — and we would
see, in Unit II, exactly where that line is.* This lesson is that line. We ask what makes
data "big," what actually breaks when it outgrows one machine, and — in the lab — we make one
of those challenges, **volume**, something you can *feel*: store a million rows two ways and
measure the gap.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy: counting Puerto Rico"}
Imagine counting every form on the island. One option is a single, very fast clerk who reads
every form (scale **up** — buy a bigger machine). The other is to have each of the 78
municipalities count its own forms locally and mail in one subtotal (scale **out** — use many
machines). Most of big data is variations on the second idea: split the work, compute where
the data already is, and assemble the answer.
:::

## The Vs of Big Data

"Big data" classically means data that is challenging along a few axes. The original three —
with a fourth your syllabus emphasizes:

| V | The challenge | What breaks on one machine |
|---|---------------|----------------------------|
| **Volume** | too much data | does not fit on disk or in RAM; a single pass takes hours or days |
| **Velocity** | arriving too fast | ingestion cannot keep up; the analysis is stale before it finishes |
| **Variety** | mixed shapes at once | one rigid schema cannot hold tables, JSON, and free text together |
| **Veracity** | quality varies by source | cleaning (already most of the work) multiplies with every new source |

The first three are the classic trio; **veracity** is the commonly added fourth, and it bites
hardest at scale because every source you bolt on brings its own errors and gaps.

## Data Shapes: the "Variety" Problem

Variety is really L01's data-shape taxonomy seen at scale:

| Shape | Example | Fits a table? |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| **Structured** | a sales table with fixed columns | yes — rows and columns |
| **Semi-structured** | JSON from a web API; tags per record vary | partly — needs flattening |
| **Unstructured** | free-text reviews, images, audio | no — needs features extracted first |

A single relational table holds the first cleanly, the second awkwardly, and the third not at
all — which is why "big data" needs more than one kind of store (the subject of **L05**).

## The Single-Machine Ceiling

Two honest observations before anyone reaches for a cluster.

First, **the ceiling is high.** One modern laptop with pandas comfortably handles datasets in
the hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes; a tuned single machine handles tens of GB. The
million-row table in the lab is *not* big data — it runs in milliseconds — and that is the
point: you should know where the real ceiling is before paying for a cluster.

Second, when you *do* cross the ceiling, **moving the data becomes the enemy.** Copying tens
of terabytes to one computer is hours of network time before any analysis begins. The cure
inverts the usual flow:

- **Scale up** — a bigger single machine (more RAM, more cores). Simple, but there is a
  hard limit, and big machines cost more than linearly.
- **Scale out** — many ordinary machines working in parallel. The data is split across them,
  and the computation is **moved to where each piece lives** instead of the data being moved
  to the computation.

Scaling out is what makes "big data" a distinct discipline; **L04** shows the mechanics.

## The Big-Data Platform Landscape

When one machine is not enough, the work splits into a few categories of tooling. This table
is also a map of the rest of Unit II:

| Need | Platform category | Where you meet it |
|------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Store data too big for one disk | distributed file systems (Hadoop / HDFS) | **L04** |
| Compute over data split across machines | cluster engines (MapReduce, **Spark**) | **L04** |
| Query structured data; flexible non-tabular stores | **SQL** databases and **NoSQL** stores | **L05** |
| Pull data in from the web | **REST APIs**, JSON over HTTP | **L06** |

You do not need a cluster for any lesson in this course — but you do need to recognize which
category a real problem calls for, and that is what Unit II builds.

## One Challenge Up Close: Storage at Volume

You will save and reload datasets constantly, and the **format** you choose changes both how
big the file is and how fast every later read runs — for free, just by picking well. Two
formats anchor the lab:

- **CSV** is plain text, one record per line. Universal — every tool and human can read it —
  but everything is stored as text (types re-inferred on every read), there is no compression,
  and to answer a question about one column the reader must scan **every byte of every row**.
- **Parquet** is a binary format that stores data **by column**, with types and per-column
  compression. To average one column it reads **only that column**, already typed and
  compressed; it can skip the rest entirely. The cost: it is binary, so you need a
  Parquet-aware reader (pandas does it) rather than a text editor.

::: {.callout-note title="Why columnar is cheaper"}
A question like *"average amount per category"* touches two columns out of five. CSV, stored
row by row, must still read all five to get there. Parquet, stored column by column, reads the
two it needs and ignores the others. The lab measures both the size gap and this column-pruning
effect on a million rows.
:::

## Which Format When

- **Reach for CSV** when: exchanging data with anyone, the file is tiny, a human must read or
  hand-edit it, or the receiving tool only accepts text.
- **Reach for Parquet** when: you will analyze the data more than once, it is large, your
  queries touch a few columns, or it feeds a pipeline.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"My 50 GB CSV — is that big data?"** — Almost certainly not. Convert it to Parquet, point
pandas (or a single-machine database) at it, and it is an ordinary dataset on one computer.
*"Does not fit in Excel"* is not the bar; *"does not fit on a machine"* is.

**"Can I open a Parquet file in Excel?"** — Not directly; it is binary. Open it with pandas.
That readability tradeoff is exactly the price you pay for the size and speed — which is why
CSV is still the right call for small files a human needs to read.
